headline: Polysilicon: The Hidden Link Between America’s Solar and Chip Industries
subtitle: New solar tariffs, signed Aug. 6 — but the real target is chips.
heading: Three things to know
bullets: Chips use just 2.4% of the world's polysilicon. Solar uses nearly all the rest.
The U.S. had ~50% of global polysilicon capacity in 2005. Under 2% by 2024.
Price floors and a 15% tariff take effect Dec. 4.
caption:
The tariffs signed on Aug. 6 are written as a solar policy. The industry they are built to rescue makes semiconductors.

Polysilicon is the shared input. Solar panels take nearly all of it; chipmakers take about 2.4% of world output, at a purity solar does not need. The same furnaces and the same trained crews serve both, which is why a plant that loses its solar orders cannot simply switch to the chip market and survive on it.

The United States held roughly half of global polysilicon capacity in 2005. By 2024 it was under 2%, after Chinese producers scaled up and prices fell below Western production costs.

The order sets a price floor and a 15% tariff, both taking effect Dec. 4. The Commerce Department frames it as rebuilding a supply chain the CHIPS Act left untouched.

Solar installers say the floor raises panel costs at the moment utility demand is climbing, and that the domestic polysilicon it protects would take years to reach the volumes chipmakers actually need.

What is unsettled is whether a price floor can hold capacity in place long enough for that to happen, or whether it only raises the cost of the panels the country is still buying from abroad.
